contract.proves:
A platform upgrade must be decided by the release manifest, and one odd
package must not fail the whole platform.

PLATFORM VERSION IS NOT PACKAGE VERSION. release-index.json is the platform
truth; the version of any individual package is not. Collapsing the two is a
standing rule violation, and it is easy to do accidentally because most
packages happen to move together.

THE FAILURE THIS ENCODES. platform_upgrade.dispatch parsed EVERY package
version as strict semver and failed the entire step when one did not parse —
ffmpeg, which is versioned by its upstream and never agreed to semver
(release.platform_upgrade_dispatch_rejects_non_semver_versions). One
third-party package with an unusual version string blocked the platform
upgrade for every service in the release. This is a dependency-shaped bug:
something non-critical placed on the critical path.

Day-0 reads release-index.json. Day-1 joins from the ACTIVE BOM, not from
latest — a node joining mid-upgrade must land on the release the cluster is
actually running, or it arrives already drifted and the first reconcile
fights the join.

Truth comes from the manifest, never from filenames. A directory listing that
looks like a version is not a version.

WHAT THIS PINS. The release boundary is intact: the platform has exactly one
active release, every node agrees on it, and the packages inside it resolve.
It is deliberately an observation of the steady state — a platform upgrade is
too destructive to drive from a test suite against a live cluster, and the
property worth guarding is that the boundary never goes ambiguous, not that a
particular upgrade succeeds.
